items.title: release-tools
items.text:
The shared release automation of Algorithmiq repositories: release branches, pre-releases (alphas, betas, release candidates), the release PR, release tags, backports, the changelog and the PR checks.

Each repository keeps three short caller stubs, its own publish workflow (because that depends on how the project is built) and a changelog preview recipe. Everything else lives in release-tools, once, and is pinned by tag.

items.title: Where to start
items.text:
• You work in a repository that uses release-tools: The release process, then Releasing and Patch releases. The branching model shows a whole release cycle.
  • You are adopting release-tools in a repository: Adopting release-tools, Per-repository setup, and once per organisation the One-time organisation setup.
  • You maintain release-tools: What is central, Versioning and upgrading, Design, Caveats, Open questions and Developing release-tools.

items.title: Adopting release-tools
items.text: Copy these files, replace v1.2.0 with the current release of release-tools (v1.2.0 or later: the stage input is new in v1.2.0), and use the same tag everywhere. The triggers stay in the stubs: only a repository's own workflow files react to its events. The bot's client ID and private key are passed explicitly rather than through vars inheritance or secrets: inherit: the reusable workflows declare them as a required input and a required secret, so a stub that forgets one fails before anything runs, and no other secret of the repository reaches release-tools.

items.title: Let an agent do it
items.text:
Repository admins can hand the adoption to a coding agent with the adopt-release-tools agent skill, which ships in skills/adopt-release-tools:

npx skills add Algorithmiq/release-tools --skill adopt-release-tools

or copy that folder into your agent's skills directory. Then ask the agent to adopt release-tools in your repository. It reads the repository and these pages at the latest release, writes the files and opens the adoption PR; you run every command that changes GitHub, from the commands it prepares. It follows this page and Per-repository setup, which stay the reference.

items.title: .github/workflows/release.yml
items.text:
version-files is a list of the files that the release bot updates for each release. Use an empty value when the version is from the git tags (setuptools-scm, hatch-vcs). Then each build that can read the tags has the exact version. This includes the wheels. You do not edit files when you make a release. Add a file to the list only when a build cannot read the tags but must have a real version:

  • The version is from the tags, and no other file contains it: "".
  • A different file contains the version, and nothing reads that file, for example a VERSION file that a person updates: "". Remove the file.
  • CMake reads the file, for a C++ header or a package configuration: "". In CMake, use the version from the tags:
  • in a scikit-build-core build, use SKBUILD_PROJECT_VERSION and SKBUILD_PROJECT_VERSION_FULL;
  • in a plain CMake build, use git describe, or a module that uses it.
  • A build without git metadata reads the file, usually a Nix derivation: the path of the file, for example "VERSION". The derivation builds without .git, and gives the file to setuptools-scm as SETUPTOOLS_SCM_PRETEND_VERSION. The bot writes the file:
  • the commit of each release tag contains the version of that release;
  • release/X.Y contains its newest final release;
  • after each X.Y.0, the changelog PR writes X.(Y+1).0.dev0 on main.
  • pyproject.toml has a static [project] version: "pyproject.toml". The bot updates it in the same way.

stage sets the first stage of a release: alpha, beta or rc. It also changes a release in beta to release candidates. Refer to Releasing.

# Releases: see https://github.com/Algorithmiq/release-tools#readme
name: Release

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      bump:
        description: "Release to start: next minor or major (patch releases: add the backport label to the fix PR)"
        type: choice
        options: [minor, major]
        default: minor
      stage:
        description: "Stage to start at or promote to (patch releases have no pre-releases)"
        type: choice
        options: [rc, beta, alpha]
        default: rc
  push:
    branches: ["release/**"]
    tags: ["v*", "!v*.dev*"]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  release:
    uses: Algorithmiq/release-tools/.github/workflows/release.yml@v1.2.0
    with:
      client-id: ${{ vars.RELEASE_BOT_CLIENT_ID }}
      bump: ${{ inputs.bump }}
      stage: ${{ inputs.stage }}
      # Files that hold the version (e.g. "VERSION pyproject.toml"); empty if it
      # comes from the git tag (setuptools-scm, hatch-vcs).
      version-files: ""
    secrets:
      private-key: ${{ secrets.RELEASE_BOT_PRIVATE_KEY }}

name: PR checks

on:
  pull_request_target:
    types: [opened, edited, reopened, synchronize]

permissions:

items.title: The publish workflow
items.text:
It must follow this structure: run on push: tags: ["v*", "!v*.dev*"] (every release tag, but not the development tags of main, which publish nothing), build and check that the built version matches the tag, write the software bills of materials (SBOMs) of the runtime dependencies and check their licenses, create a draft GitHub release with every file attached, publish to PyPI with Trusted Publishing, and publish the GitHub release last. The build stays the repository's own; the SBOM, the license check and the three release steps are actions from here. The release-notes action needs the full history and tags (fetch-depth: 0), and the release jobs need contents: write; the job that calls release-notes also needs pull-requests: read, which it uses to read the PR descriptions of a pre-release. The jobs that only call GitHub or the package index run on ubuntu-slim, the one-CPU runner for short jobs (15 minutes at most, no Docker). build and sbom install the project, and upload_pypi runs a Docker action, so they stay on ubuntu-latest. A complete example:

# Publishing: see https://github.com/Algorithmiq/release-tools#readme
#
# Runs on the v* tags that the release workflow pushes: build, draft the GitHub release
# with every file attached, publish to PyPI, then publish the GitHub release, which makes
# it immutable. Never on `release: published`. Only the build job is repository-specific.
name: Publish

on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*", "!v*.dev*"]

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  # A publish run must never be cut short half-way through.
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  build:
    name: Build sdist and wheel
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v10.3.2
      - name: Build distributions
        run: uv build --out-dir dist
      - name: Check the version matches the release tag
        run: |
          expected="${GITHUB_REF_NAME#v}"
          wheels=(dist/*.whl)
          actual="$(basename "${wheels[0]}" | cut -d- -f2)"
          if [[ "$actual" != "$expected" ]]; then
            echo "::error::built version is '$actual', but the release tag is '$expected'"
            exit 1
          fi
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7.0.2
        with:
          name: dist
          path: dist/*

  sbom:
    # The software bills of materials of the locked runtime dependencies, attached to the
    # release, and their licenses checked: a failure stops the release before the draft
    # exists. A separate artifact: the upload takes everything in dist/.
    name: SBOM and license check
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1
      - uses: Algorithmiq/release-tools/actions/sbom@v1.2.0
      - uses: Algorithmiq/release-tools/actions/license-check@v1.2.0
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7.0.2
        with:
          name: sbom
          path: sbom/*

  draft_release:
    # Immutable releases: files can only be attached while the release is a draft.
    name: Create the draft GitHub release
    needs: [build, sbom]
    runs-on: ubuntu-slim
    permissions:
      contents: write
      pull-requests: read  # release-notes reads the PR descriptions
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0  # git-cliff needs the full history and the tags
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8.0.2
        with:
          name: dist
          path: dist
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8.0.2
        with:
          name: sbom
          path: sbom
      - id: notes
        uses: Algorithmiq/release-tools/actions/release-notes@v1.2.0
      - uses: Algorithmiq/release-tools/actions/draft-release@v1.2.0
        with:
          notes-file: ${{ steps.notes.outputs.path }}
          files: |
            dist/*
            sbom/*

  upload_pypi:
    name: Upload to PyPI
    needs: draft_release
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: pypi
    permissions:
      id-token: write
      attestations: write
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8.0.2
        with:
          name: dist
          path: dist
      - uses: actions/attest-build-provenance@v4.2.2
        with:
          subject-path: "dist/*"
      - uses: pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish@v1.14.3

  publish_release:
    # Publishing locks the tag and the files and creates GitHub's release attestation.
    name: Publish the GitHub release
    needs: upload_pypi
    runs-on: ubuntu-slim
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - uses: Algorithmiq/release-tools/actions/publish-release@v1.2.0

release-notes writes the tag's section of CHANGELOG.md for a final release, as the release PR left it with its wording fixes (if the file has no section for the tag, a warning says so and git cliff --current writes the notes from the commits). For a pre-release it writes everything since the last final release (git cliff --unreleased --tag vX.Y.0rcN), with each change's Migration section taken from its PR description (see Caveats). It outputs the file's path. draft-release takes notes-file and files (one glob per line, each must match), and marks alphas, betas and release candidates as pre-releases. publish-release publishes the draft. All three default to the tag that triggered the run (tag input) and to github.token (token input). release-notes installs git-cliff itself, the official binary with its checksum verified, with taiki-e/install-action.

items.title: Software bills of materials
items.text:
The organisation's secure development policy asks for a software bill of materials of each released package. The sbom job writes one with the sbom action, in CycloneDX JSON, and draft_release attaches it to the release next to the distributions.

  • What it lists: the runtime dependencies locked in uv.lock. Each SBOM comes from a scratch environment that uv sync --frozen --no-default-groups --no-install-project creates, so it leaves out the dependency groups (tests, docs) and the project itself, which is the SBOM's root component. cyclonedx-py environment reads each package's licenses from its installed metadata, which uv export --format cyclonedx1.5 doesn't provide.
  • flavours: one SBOM per line, a name and its uv sync arguments, for a package whose extras pull in more dependencies:
- uses: Algorithmiq/release-tools/actions/sbom@v1.2.0
  with:
    flavours: |
      core
      viz --extra viz

writes <project>-core.cdx.json and <project>-viz.cdx.json. Without flavours, one SBOM without extras: <project>.cdx.json. - Other inputs: path, the directory (default sbom, which the action outputs as path); component-type, library (the default) or application; and version, the root component's version when pyproject.toml has none (setuptools-scm, hatch-vcs), which defaults to the tag. - One platform: the environment is the runner's. Dependencies behind platform markers (sys_platform == "win32") may differ on other platforms; a project that ships platform wheels can run the job once per platform, with a different path and artifact name for each. - Needs a uv project with uv.lock. The action sets up uv itself, without a cache, in the version pyproject.toml or uv.toml requires, if any. A project whose dependencies come from a private index gives the sbom job the same credentials as its build.

items.title: License check
items.text:
The same policy asks for a check, before each release, that no dependency's license clashes with how the package ships. The license-check action runs anchore/grant, at a pinned version whose checksum it verifies, on the SBOMs: a license outside the policy, or a package without any license, fails the sbom job, so the release stops before its draft exists.

  • policy: a preset of release-tools, at the version the action is pinned to. open-source (the default, in actions/license-check/policies) allows what an Apache-2.0 library may depend on: permissive licenses and weak copyleft (LGPL, MPL). A repository can instead give the path of its own grant configuration, used as it is.
  • ignore-packages: the repository's reviewed exceptions, one per line as name: reason; every entry needs the reason it passes:
- uses: Algorithmiq/release-tools/actions/license-check@v1.2.0
  with:
    ignore-packages: |
      block2: GPL-3.0-only, run as a separate program, never imported

ignore-packages-file reads more of them from a file in the repository, in the same format, so that the publish workflow and licenses.yml share one list. - sboms: the SBOMs to check, one glob per line (default sbom/*.cdx.json). - An OR expression passes only if every alternative is allowed: grant checks each one. A package offering LGPL-3.0-only OR GPL-3.0-only fails, and goes into ignore-packages with the option the project takes.

items.title: Licenses on pull requests
items.text:
licenses.yml runs the same two actions on the pull requests that change pyproject.toml or uv.lock, so that a license outside the policy shows up when the dependency is added rather than at release time. It runs on pull_request, with the PR's own code and a read-only token; unlike pr-checks.yml, which runs on pull_request_target and must never read the PR's files.

# Licenses: see https://github.com/Algorithmiq/release-tools#readme
#
# The publish workflow's SBOM and license check, on the pull requests that change the
# dependencies: a license outside the policy shows up before release time.
name: Licenses

on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - pyproject.toml
      - uv.lock
      - .github/workflows/licenses.yml
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  licenses:
    name: SBOM and license check
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1
      - uses: Algorithmiq/release-tools/actions/sbom@v1.2.0
      - uses: Algorithmiq/release-tools/actions/license-check@v1.2.0

items.title: Publishing to AWS CodeArtifact
items.text:
A package for the organisation's private index on AWS CodeArtifact keeps the same structure. Its upload job assumes the upload role with GitHub's OIDC token and runs uv publish; the CODEARTIFACT_* variables come from the organisation (One-time organisation setup, step 5), so no repository's pyproject.toml changes. A build that needs private dependencies assumes vars.CODEARTIFACT_READ_ROLE the same way before building.

  • A failed upload can be re-run. The job hands uv the index as a configuration file (--index), and uv reads it with the same credentials to skip the files already there. UV_PUBLISH_URL with --check-url alone doesn't do this for a private index: uv reads the check URL without credentials.
  • No PEP 740 attestations (--no-attestations): they are verified and served by indexes with Trusted Publishing, such as PyPI, and CodeArtifact has none. The job attests the files with GitHub's build provenance instead, which works with any index: gh attestation verify <file> --owner Algorithmiq. In private and internal repositories this needs GitHub Enterprise Cloud.
# Publishing to AWS CodeArtifact: see https://github.com/Algorithmiq/release-tools#readme
#
# Runs on the v* tags that the release workflow pushes: build, draft the GitHub release
# with every file attached, upload to the organisation's private package index on AWS
# CodeArtifact, then publish the GitHub release, which makes it immutable. Never on
# `release: published`. Only the build job is repository-specific; the CODEARTIFACT_*
# variables are set once for the organisation.
name: Publish

on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*", "!v*.dev*"]

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  # A publish run must never be cut short half-way through.
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  build:
    name: Build sdist and wheel
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v10.3.2
      - name: Build distributions
        run: uv build --out-dir dist
      - name: Check the version matches the release tag
        run: |
          expected="${GITHUB_REF_NAME#v}"
          wheels=(dist/*.whl)
          actual="$(basename "${wheels[0]}" | cut -d- -f2)"
          if [[ "$actual" != "$expected" ]]; then
            echo "::error::built version is '$actual', but the release tag is '$expected'"
            exit 1
          fi
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7.0.2
        with:
          name: dist
          path: dist/*

  sbom:
    # The software bills of materials of the locked runtime dependencies, attached to the
    # release, and their licenses checked: a failure stops the release before the draft
    # exists. A separate artifact: the upload takes everything in dist/.
    name: SBOM and license check
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1
      - uses: Algorithmiq/release-tools/actions/sbom@v1.2.0
      - uses: Algorithmiq/release-tools/actions/license-check@v1.2.0
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7.0.2
        with:
          name: sbom
          path: sbom/*

  draft_release:
    # Immutable releases: files can only be attached while the release is a draft.
    name: Create the draft GitHub release
    needs: [build, sbom]
    runs-on: ubuntu-slim
    permissions:
      contents: write
      pull-requests: read  # release-notes reads the PR descriptions
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0  # git-cliff needs the full history and the tags
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8.0.2
        with:
          name: dist
          path: dist
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8.0.2
        with:
          name: sbom
          path: sbom
      - id: notes
        uses: Algorithmiq/release-tools/actions/release-notes@v1.2.0
      - uses: Algorithmiq/release-tools/actions/draft-release@v1.2.0
        with:
          notes-file: ${{ steps.notes.outputs.path }}
          files: |
            dist/*
            sbom/*

  upload_codeartifact:
    name: Upload to AWS CodeArtifact
    needs: draft_release
    runs-on: ubuntu-slim
    permissions:
      id-token: write  # the upload role and the attestations use GitHub's OIDC token
      attestations: write
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8.0.2
        with:
          name: dist
          path: dist
      # Build provenance, stored by GitHub: `gh attestation verify <file> --owner <org>`.
      - uses: actions/attest-build-provenance@v4.2.2
        with:
          subject-path: "dist/*"
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6.3.0
        with:
          role-to-assume: ${{ vars.CODEARTIFACT_WRITE_ROLE }}
          aws-region: ${{ vars.CODEARTIFACT_REGION }}
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v10.3.2
        with:
          enable-cache: false
      - name: Upload with uv publish
        env:
          DOMAIN: ${{ vars.CODEARTIFACT_DOMAIN }}
          DOMAIN_OWNER: ${{ vars.CODEARTIFACT_DOMAIN_OWNER }}
          REPOSITORY: ${{ vars.CODEARTIFACT_REPOSITORY }}
        run: |
          token="$(aws codeartifact get-authorization-token \
            --domain "$DOMAIN" --domain-owner "$DOMAIN_OWNER" \
            --query authorizationToken --output text)"
          echo "::add-mask::$token"
          endpoint="$(aws codeartifact get-repository-endpoint \
            --domain "$DOMAIN" --domain-owner "$DOMAIN_OWNER" --repository "$REPOSITORY" \
            --format pypi --query repositoryEndpoint --output text)"
          endpoint="${endpoint%/}/"
          # With --index, uv reads the index, with its credentials, and skips the files
          # already there, so a failed run can be re-run.
          config="$RUNNER_TEMP/codeartifact.toml"
          printf '[[index]]\nname = "codeartifact"\nurl = "%s"\npublish-url = "%s"\nexplicit = true\n' \
            "${endpoint}simple/" "$endpoint" > "$config"
          export UV_INDEX_CODEARTIFACT_USERNAME=aws UV_INDEX_CODEARTIFACT_PASSWORD="$token"
          uv publish --config-file "$config" --index codeartifact \
            --trusted-publishing never --no-attestations dist/*

  publish_release:
    # Publishing locks the tag and the files and creates GitHub's release attestation.
    name: Publish the GitHub release
    needs: upload_codeartifact
    runs-on: ubuntu-slim
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - uses: Algorithmiq/release-tools/actions/publish-release@v1.2.0

items.title: Linters and formatters: leave out CHANGELOG.md
items.text:
The release PR and the changelog PR write CHANGELOG.md. git-cliff copies the summary and the Migration section of each PR into it, code blocks included. Nobody formats this text for your linters. If a linter or a formatter checks CHANGELOG.md, a bot PR can fail a required check, and the release stops until somebody edits the bot's branch. For example, ruff format also formats the Python code blocks in Markdown files: one Migration example without a blank line after its imports makes the release PR fail lint.

Leave CHANGELOG.md out of every tool that checks its contents:

  • pre-commit or prek: the top-level exclude of the configuration. It applies to every hook. Add the file to an existing regex with |.
exclude: ^CHANGELOG\.md$
  • ruff: extend-exclude in [tool.ruff] of pyproject.toml, or in ruff.toml. It keeps the default exclusions of ruff. It applies to ruff format . and to the hooks of ruff-pre-commit, because those hooks use --force-exclude. If the configuration sets exclude, add the file there.
[tool.ruff]
extend-exclude = ["CHANGELOG.md"]
  • Other tools that a workflow starts directly (prettier, markdownlint, mdformat, typos, codespell): the ignore list of each tool, for example .prettierignore.

items.title: justfile: preview the changelog
items.text:
just changelog shows what the next release's entry will look like, with the central cliff.toml at the version the stubs pin (read from release.yml, so Dependabot's updates carry over). It reads the squash commits, so a Migration section shows as the commit has it (wrapped, if it was merged in the web UI), not as the release PR will take it from the PR description (see Caveats). If release-tools is public:

git_cliff := "git-cliff==2.14.2"

# Preview the changelog entry of the next release, with the central cliff.toml at the version release.yml pins.
changelog:
    #!/usr/bin/env bash
    set -euo pipefail
    ref=$(sed -nE 's|.*Algorithmiq/release-tools/.github/workflows/release.yml@([^[:space:]]+).*|\1|p' \
        .github/workflows/release.yml)
    # Link the PR numbers like the release PR does: GitHub Actions sets GITHUB_REPOSITORY.
    repo=$(git remote get-url origin | sed -E 's#^.*github\.com[:/]##; s#\.git$##')
    GITHUB_REPOSITORY="${GITHUB_REPOSITORY:-$repo}" uvx --from {{ git_cliff }} git-cliff --unreleased \
        --config-url "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Algorithmiq/release-tools/$ref/cliff.toml"

--config-url only works for a public repository. If release-tools is internal or private, fetch the file with the GitHub CLI instead (any member who has run gh auth login):

git_cliff := "git-cliff==2.14.2"

# Preview the changelog entry of the next release, with the central cliff.toml at the version release.yml pins.
changelog:
    #!/usr/bin/env bash
    set -euo pipefail
    ref=$(sed -nE 's|.*Algorithmiq/release-tools/.github/workflows/release.yml@([^[:space:]]+).*|\1|p' \
        .github/workflows/release.yml)
    # release-tools isn't public: fetch cliff.toml with the GitHub CLI (`gh auth login`).
    config="$(mktemp -d)/cliff.toml"
    gh api -H "Accept: application/vnd.github.raw" \
        "repos/Algorithmiq/release-tools/contents/cliff.toml?ref=$ref" > "$config"
    # Link the PR numbers like the release PR does: GitHub Actions sets GITHUB_REPOSITORY.
    repo=$(git remote get-url origin | sed -E 's#^.*github\.com[:/]##; s#\.git$##')
    GITHUB_REPOSITORY="${GITHUB_REPOSITORY:-$repo}" uvx --from {{ git_cliff }} git-cliff --unreleased \
        --config "$config"

items.title: PR template
items.text:
The changelog copies the PR description's ## Migration section, up to the next ## heading, into the PR's entry. Breaking changes and deprecations need it; any other change that users must act on (a stub to update, say) can have one too. Keep the section above any later heading of the template (such as a checklist), so that only the notes are copied, and never make it the last thing in the description (see Caveats). The release PR and the release notes of a pre-release read it from the PR description itself, which needs the pull-requests: read permission of the publish workflow:

<!-- Keep this section above the Checklist: the changelog takes everything up to the next heading. -->
## Migration
<!-- Required for breaking changes (!) and deprecations. For any other change, only if
     users must act on it. Delete otherwise. The changelog shows it under the entry.
     What do users need to change? Show a before/after example if possible. -->

## Checklist

- [ ] Bug fix for the current release: add the `backport` label (or ask a maintainer to)

items.title: Branching model
items.text:
release/X.Y is created at the feature freeze: the first beta, or the first release candidate when there are no betas. Alphas never create a branch. Each step below is the same history, later.

1. v1.1.0 is out. release/1.1 was cut at v1.1.0rc1; merging its release PR tagged v1.1.0, and the changelog was copied back to main. Features keep landing on main. The bot tags the changelog commit v1.2.0.dev0, and writes that version into main's version files if the repository has any: v1.1.0 is never in main's history, so without it versions derived from main (setuptools-scm, hatch-vcs, copier) would sort below v1.1.0. The tag is a development marker, not a release: nothing publishes it.

  branch release/1.1
  commit id: "release v1.1.0" tag: "v1.1.0"
  checkout main
  commit id: "changelog v1.1.0" tag: "v1.2.0.dev0"
  commit id: "feat: B"

2. Alphas. Release, minor, alpha tags main's HEAD; each rerun tags the next alpha. No branch, no release PR. Features keep landing.

3. Beta: the feature freeze. Release, minor, beta cuts release/1.2 at main's HEAD and tags v1.2.0b1; the release PR opens as a draft. feat: E lands on main after the freeze, so it waits for 1.3. fix: F gets the backport label: because 1.2 is in pre-release, it goes to both lines, tagging v1.2.0b2 and updating the v1.1.1 release PR, which a maintainer merges.

4. Release candidates. Release, minor, rc promotes 1.2: it tags v1.2.0rc1 on the branch HEAD (the same commit as v1.2.0b2) and marks the release PR ready. The next backport, fix: G, tags v1.2.0rc2 and still reaches 1.1 (pending v1.1.2).

items.title: Versions of main
items.text:
A development build of main is, for example, a nightly build, pip install git+…@main, or an editable install. This build finds its version in one of two locations:

  • the nearest v* tag in the history of main (setuptools-scm, hatch-vcs, git describe, copier);
  • the version files, with version-files.

These two locations do not contain the versions of the release line. The final tags are only on release/X.Y. The betas and the release candidates after the freeze are also only on release/X.Y. With version files, each pre-release tag points to a commit that is not on main. This commit records the version, and the bot does not push it to a branch.

Thus, after each X.Y.0, the bot changes main to the next series. It tags the commit that the changelog PR adds to main with vX.(Y+1).0.dev0. It also writes this version into the version files.

A .dev version is a pre-release, and nothing publishes it. It is lower than each alpha, beta and release candidate of its version. It is higher than each release before it: 1.1.2 < 1.2.0.dev0 < 1.2.0a1. The tag identifies the next minor release, because the bot cannot know if the next release is a major release. The order stays correct: 1.2.0.dev0 is also lower than 2.0.0a1.

The table shows the version of main at each step of the history above. For versions from tags, the table uses setuptools-scm, one or two commits after the newest tag in the history of main.

Step Newest release of the line main, version from tags main, version files 1. v1.1.0 is out 1.1.0 1.2.0.dev1: higher 1.2.0.dev0: higher 2. Alphas 1.2.0a2 1.2.0a3.dev1: higher 1.2.0.dev0: lower 3. Beta, the freeze 1.2.0b2 1.2.0b2.dev1: lower 1.2.0.dev0: lower 4. Release candidates 1.2.0rc2 1.2.0b2.dev2: lower 1.2.0.dev0: lower 5. v1.2.0 and its patches 1.2.1 1.3.0.dev1: higher 1.3.0.dev0: higher

items.title: Known problems
items.text:
In four cases, the version of main is not correct. The examples use the history above.

Problem Steps Builds with the problem main shows The release line has 1. The freeze 3, 4 Version from tags 1.2.0b2.devN 1.2.0b2, 1.2.0rc2 2. Version files 2, 3, 4 Version files 1.2.0.dev0 1.2.0a2 to 1.2.0rc2 3. A late changelog PR 5 Version from tags 1.2.0b2.devN 1.2.0 4. A major release 5 All 1.3.0.devN Next release: 2.0.0

items.title: 1. The freeze
items.text:
From the cut of release/1.2 to 1.2.0, main shows 1.2.0b2.devN. This version has two errors:

  • it is lower than the betas and release candidates of release/1.2;
  • it identifies the 1.2 series, but the changes on main after the cut go into 1.3.

Cause: the newest tag in the history of main is v1.2.0b1. This tag is on the commit where release/1.2 starts. setuptools-scm calculates the version from this tag.

Why the bot does not tag main at the cut: the commit at the cut is also in the history of release/1.2. A v1.3.0.dev0 tag on this commit also changes the versions of release/1.2 to 1.3.0.devN.

items.title: 2. Version files
items.text:
This problem applies only to a build that reads its version from the version files. This is usually a build without git metadata, for example a Nix derivation (refer to Adopting release-tools).

  • On main, the files contain 1.2.0.dev0 from 1.1.0 to 1.2.0. This version is lower than each alpha, beta and release candidate of 1.2.
  • On release/1.2, the files contain 1.2.0.dev0 until 1.2.0. After 1.2.0, they contain 1.2.0, also when backports for 1.2.1 have merged.

Cause: only a commit can change the files. The bot writes the files only in the release PR of a final release and in the changelog PR. For a pre-release, the bot writes the version in a commit that only the tag points to. No branch contains this commit.

items.title: 3. A late changelog PR
items.text:
After 1.2.0, the bot puts the tag v1.3.0.dev0 on the commit that the changelog PR adds to main. If the PR does not merge immediately, the job shows a warning. Until the PR merges, main shows 1.2.0b2.devN. This version is lower than 1.2.0.

Correction: merge the PR. Then start the "Release" workflow run again, to add the tag. If you do not do this, the problem stops at the first alpha of 1.3.

items.title: 4. A major release
items.text:
The bot cannot know if the next release is a major release. Thus, after 1.2.0, main shows 1.3.0.devN, also when the next release is 2.0.0. The order is correct: 1.3.0.dev1 is lower than 2.0.0a1. But the number is not correct. The number becomes correct at the first alpha, 2.0.0a1.

These problems apply only to the versions of main, and nothing publishes these versions. The problems are important when a build of main must agree with a release. For example, a test environment can require >= the latest release candidate. We accept these problems. Refer to Open questions for the reasons and the solutions that we examined.

items.title: Caveats
items.text:
• Footers. git-cliff ends the body of a commit at the first line that looks like a footer (Closes #12, **Docs:** …, Before: …) and puts the rest into the footers. cliff.toml therefore takes the Migration section from the whole message. Up to v1.5.0 it took it from the body, so a description with such a line above the section lost its notes: the release notes and CHANGELOG.md of v1.5.0 were repaired by hand.
  • Changelog entries come from the PR descriptions. GitHub's web UI wraps the body of a squash commit at 72 columns, which breaks the indented lines of a Migration section (a Python snippet fails with IndentationError) and the text that continues a list item. The release PR and the release notes of a pre-release therefore replace each commit's body by the description of its PR, with git cliff --context, the release pr-descriptions command and git cliff --from-context. One GraphQL query per 100 commits looks up the PR number that ends the commit's title ((#12)); the description counts only if the PR is merged and its merge commit is that commit.
  • If the API fails (a rate limit, a token without pull-requests: read), the PR is not found or it is not that commit's (a commit cherry-picked by hand keeps the original title and number), the commit keeps its own body and a warning in the job log names the commit and the PR. A commit pushed without a PR keeps its body as well.
  • A description edited after the merge reaches the next generated changelog: the release PR regenerates CHANGELOG.md only when something is pushed to the release branch (re-run the "Release" run of the last push to refresh it). It never reaches a release that is published.
  • A backport PR's description starts with "Backport of #N to release/X.Y." and continues with the description of the original, so a backported entry keeps its Migration section.
  • Local previews (just changelog) and runs without GITHUB_REPOSITORY read the commit bodies, as before.
  • A BREAKING CHANGE: footer that is only in the commit body no longer counts: mark breaking changes with ! in the title, as the process says.
  • The changelog PR merges itself, without a review or its checks. After a final release the bot opens a PR adding the release's section of CHANGELOG.md to main and merges it at once with its bypass of the main ruleset (gh pr merge --admin): the section was already reviewed in the release PR, and CI runs on main after the merge. Without the bypass (Per-repository setup, step 8) the job enables auto-merge instead, with a warning, and the PR waits for an approval: auto-merge never bypasses a ruleset. If a changelog PR conflicts (two finals released close together), re-run its "Release" workflow run's sync job: it checks out main, rebuilds changelog/vX.Y.Z from the current main with git checkout -B, and force-pushes it. The job opens the PR only if none is open for the branch, so with the PR still open it updates it and merges it. The merge deletes the changelog/vX.Y.Z branch (--delete-branch); if the job had to fall back to auto-merge, the branch may stay until the repository deletes it (the setting "Automatically delete head branches").
  • Linters and formatters see a generated CHANGELOG.md. The bot's release and changelog PRs write it from the PR descriptions, Migration code blocks included. A repository that adopted release-tools before v1.5.0 may still check the file with ruff format (which formats Python blocks in Markdown), a Markdown linter or a spell checker; a bot PR then fails a required check. Leave the file out of them, as Adopting release-tools shows.
  • Development tags on main. Final tags are created on release/X.Y and never reach main's history. After X.Y.0, the bot therefore tags the commit that the changelog PR adds to main with vX.(Y+1).0.dev0, so that git describe, setuptools-scm, hatch-vcs and copier see main above X.Y.0 (for example 1.3.0.dev2+g1234567). A .dev version is a pre-release under PEP 440: pip, uv and copier ignore it unless asked for pre-releases. Nothing publishes it, but it is a v* tag: every workflow on push: tags must exclude it with "!v*.dev*", as the stubs do. Otherwise the publish workflow runs for it, and the release-notes action fails with that hint. The tag needs the changelog PR merged: if the bot can't merge it at once (auto-merge or a merge by hand), the job warns, and versions derived from main stay below X.Y.0 until the PR merges and the job's "Release" run is re-run, or until the next alpha. The tag says X.(Y+1) even if the next release turns out to be a major one: it still sorts above X.Y.0 and below every pre-release of the next release. Refer to Branching model for the version of main at each step of a release cycle. It also shows the steps where this version is lower than the release line.
  • Check names. The PR checks report as PR checks / PR title and PR checks / Migration notes. A repository that required the contexts PR title and Migration notes of its own copy must switch its rulesets to the new names right after merging the stub: pull_request_target runs the workflow file of main, so the PR adding the stub still reports the old names, and every later PR the new ones.
  • Workflows on release: events no longer run. publish-release publishes the GitHub release with GITHUB_TOKEN, and events caused by GITHUB_TOKEN start no workflows. A workflow that ran on release: published (tests, a container image, documentation) runs on push: tags: ["v*", "!v*.dev*"] instead, or becomes a job of the publish workflow that publish_release needs.
  • job.workflow_* is GitHub.com-only (not on GitHub Enterprise Server), and actionlint 1.7.12 doesn't know it yet: .github/actionlint.yaml ignores the two properties in release.yml and backport.yml. Consumers' stubs don't use it.
  • The release and backport jobs check release-tools out into .release-tools/ inside the caller's working tree. It is never added to a commit: the workflow only adds CHANGELOG.md and the version files, and excludes .release-tools/ via .git/info/exclude.
  • An older release line runs its own version of the workflows. Each push to release/X.Y runs the workflow files of that branch, whose stub pins the release-tools version of the time the branch was created. A patch release of an older line therefore runs that older release-tools (for release-tools itself: its own older workflows), with that version's behaviour and texts. Bump the pin on an older line only if its patch releases need a fix of release-tools.
  • Changelog entries of backports link the backport PR. The changelog lists the PR that was squash-merged into each branch: a fix backported to two lines appears as, say, #15 under one and #16 under the other, not as the original PR on main. Each backport PR's description links the original ("Backport of #14").
  • The notes of a final release are the section of CHANGELOG.md at the tag. They carry the wording fixes made in the release PR. A fix to CHANGELOG.md made after the merge, on main or anywhere else, does not reach a published release: its notes are immutable. A repository whose release PRs do not add a section for the tag (for example, one that never committed CHANGELOG.md) gets a warning, and the notes come from the commits with git cliff --current.
  • Concurrency. The release jobs queue per ref in the group release-<ref> of the calling repository. A promotion runs in main's group, so a backport merged into release/X.Y at the same moment may briefly leave the release PR or a beta tag out of step; the next push to the branch puts the PR right.
  • A run can be dropped. GitHub keeps only one pending run per group: when three pushes to release/X.Y come in quick succession, the run of the second one is cancelled. If that push was the merge of the release PR, no final tag is created. The next run finds the release commit below its HEAD, without its tag, and stops with an error that names the version and the commit: it tags nothing and leaves the release PR alone. To recover, re-run the cancelled "Release" run from the Actions tab: it checks out the commit of its own push, the release commit, and tags the final release there. Then re-run the failed run: it opens the release PR of the next patch release for the commits after the release commit. The run of the first push works as usual on its own commit, below the release commit. If it updates the release PR after the merge, it reopens it, and the PR goes with the deletion of its branch release-pr/X.Y when the final is tagged. To avoid all this, wait for the run of a push to finish before pushing again to the branch, above all around the merge of a release PR.
